title: The Proxy Trap
author: Didau, David
summary: David Didau revisits the 'poor proxies for learning' argument he helped crystallize in 2013 and engages with a challenge from critic Jon Brunskill. In the era before 2013, English teachers were evaluated on surface features—busyness, pace, group work—rather than actual durable learning, distorting instruction toward performance. Rob Coe's 2013 lecture named engagement, written work, calm classrooms, and correct answers as potentially poor proxies, not because they are worthless, but because they cannot bear the inferential weight placed on them. Didau concedes Brunskill's point that the phrase has been misused and that the evidence-informed movement has generated its own new proxies. However, he argues the answer is 'proxy humility'—using multiple lines of evidence while distrusting any single indicator, including those favored by the current evidence movement. The core pathology, he concludes, has never been the existence of proxies but our insatiable hunger for easy reassurance that short-circuits genuine inquiry.
points: Before 2013, English lesson observations graded teachers on visible surface features—busyness, pace, group work—that had near-zero reliability and bore little relationship to whether students actually retained learning.

Rob Coe's influential 2013 lecture listed engagement, written output, calm classrooms, and correct answers as examples of poor proxies—not worthless in themselves, but unable to bear the inferential conclusions placed on them.
Graded lesson observation had extraordinarily low inter-rater reliability: if one observer rated a lesson inadequate, there was a 90% chance a second observer would give a different grade.

The evidence-informed movement has generated its own new proxies—'thinking hard,' retrieval practice, cold calling, knowledge organisers—that can be performed as theater without producing durable learning.
The solution is proxy humility: continue observing lessons and checking books, but always distrust easy inferences, recognizing that any single visible trace can be stage-managed.
quotes: Lesson observation, at least as commonly enacted, distorted teaching, pushed teachers to focus on performance rather than learning, and created a system more interested in short-term fluff than real improvement.
Schools had become too confident that learning could be recognised by its surface features.

if one observer judged a lesson outstanding, the probability that a second observer would give a different grade was between 51% and 78%. If a lesson was judged inadequate, there was a 90% chance that a second observer would grade it differently.
These myths are like bindweed. It's not enough to root them out once, we have to contintually guard against them growing back.
Proxy worship writes policies, designs learning walk protocols, produces book scrutiny pro formas and shapes appraisal targets.
The lesson, then, is that the poor proxies argument has to be turned on itself.
We should always distrust easy inferences but even scepticism can become lazy. We need proxies but we should never rely on them.
The enemy was never engagement, order, feedback, written work or any other visible trace of learning. The enemy has always been our insatiable hunger for easy answers.
